title: The lobster fiefs: Economic and ecological effects of territoriality in the Maine lobster industry
description: Informal territoriality ('harbor gangs'): fishermen defend perimeter-defended areas, cutting trap lines of intruders after warnings.
evidence: Defended areas have larger lobsters, higher catch and incomes.

title: An Evolutionary Approach to Norms
description: Metanorms: punish those who fail to punish defectors.
evidence: Simulations: norms collapse without metanorms, established with them.

title: Team Incentives: Evidence from a Firm Level Experiment
description: Rank incentives and team tournaments.
evidence: Stronger incentives lead workers to form teams by ability rather than friendship.

title: Local-level management and the commons problem: A comparative study of Turkish coastal fisheries
description: Rotational lottery of fishing spots: sites allocated annually by lot and fishers rotate daily through them.
evidence: Descriptive: rotation reduces conflict and equalizes access.

title: Fines, Leniency, and Rewards in Antitrust
description: Compares antitrust fines, leniency for reporters, and cash rewards for whistleblowing cartel members.
evidence: Leniency strengthens deterrence; rewards drive prices to competitive level.

field_of_use: cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus) and client fish
title: Image scoring and cooperation in a cleaner fish mutualism
description: Clients eavesdrop on cleaners' interactions and preferentially approach cleaners seen cooperating.
evidence: Cleaners behave more cooperatively when observed by bystanders.

title: On compliance
description: Managerial model: compliance achieved through transparency, reporting, capacity-building, and dispute resolution rather than coercive sanctions.
evidence: Descriptive: most states comply most of the time; noncompliance mainly from ambiguity and capacity.

title: Social Capital in the Creation of Human Capital
description: Network closure enables effective norms and sanctions, trustworthiness via obligations and expectations.
evidence: Empirical: closure associated with lower dropout rates.

field_of_use: lab repeated PD with voted payoff modification
title: Institutions and Behavior: Experimental Evidence on the Effects of Democracy
description: Subjects vote on whether to adopt a fine-like payoff modification that makes cooperation dominant; compared with random computer imposition.
evidence: The same policy raises cooperation more when chosen democratically than when exogenously imposed ('democracy premium').

title: Who Blows the Whistle on Corporate Fraud?
description: Whistleblowing by employees and other non-traditional actors; monetary rewards (qui tam) strengthen incentives to report.
evidence: Employees, media, and regulators detect much fraud; in healthcare, where qui tam rewards exist, employees blow the whistle far more often.

title: Altruistic punishment in humans
description: Altruistic punishment: costly sanctioning of free riders with no future interaction, driven by negative emotions toward defectors.
evidence: Cooperation flourishes with punishment and breaks down without it, even with perfect stranger matching.

field_of_use: lab public-goods game with group reassignment
title: Gossip and Ostracism Promote Cooperation in Groups
description: Players can gossip about past partners to future partners and groups can exclude members before each round.
evidence: Gossip plus ostracism produces the highest cooperation; gossiped-about players reform.

title: A Fine is a Price
description: Introduction of a small monetary fine for parents collecting children late.
evidence: Late arrivals increased after the fine and did not return to baseline when it was removed.

title: Sticks and Stones: Naming and Shaming the Human Rights Enforcement Problem
description: Naming and shaming by NGOs, media, and international organizations publicizing violations.
evidence: Shamed governments improve some rights (political) but continue or increase other violations (terror).

title: Antisocial Punishment Across Societies
description: Peer punishment option in public-goods games compared across societies; records punishment directed at cooperators ('antisocial punishment').
evidence: Punishment's cooperation benefit varies by society; antisocial punishment is prevalent where norms of civic cooperation and rule of law are weak.

title: Peer Pressure and Partnerships
description: Peer pressure (guilt, shame, mutual monitoring) counteracts free-riding under profit sharing.
evidence: Theoretical.

title: The Role of Market Forces in Assuring Contractual Performance
description: Price premium plus sunk, firm-specific investments (e.g., brand advertising) act as a bond forfeited if the firm cheats on quality.
evidence: Theoretical: quality assured when quasi-rents exceed short-run cheating gains.

title: Emergent Properties of Balinese Water Temple Networks: Coadaptation on a Rugged Fitness Landscape
description: Water-temple networks coordinate irrigation schedules (turn-taking) across subaks, balancing water sharing and pest control.
evidence: Simulation: temple-level coordination yields near-optimal harvests.

field_of_use: lab VCM with costless disapproval points
title: Monetary and Nonmonetary Punishment in the Voluntary Contributions Mechanism
description: Nonmonetary punishment: expressions of disapproval ('points') without payoff consequences versus monetary punishment.
evidence: Nonmonetary disapproval initially raises contributions nearly as much as monetary punishment, but monetary is more durable.

field_of_use: US DOJ Corporate Leniency Program (1993 revision)
title: Strategic Leniency and Cartel Enforcement
description: Amnesty to the first cartel member to self-report, creating a race to confess.
evidence: Cartel discoveries spike immediately after the 1993 revision and then fall below pre-program levels, consistent with deterrence.

title: Climate Clubs: Overcoming Free-riding in International Climate Policy
description: Climate club: participants adopt harmonized carbon prices and impose uniform tariffs on non-participants.
evidence: Modeling: modest tariffs can induce stable large coalitions with high abatement.

title: Covenants with and without a Sword: Self-Governance Is Possible
description: Compares face-to-face communication (covenants), peer sanctioning (sword), and both in a CPR game; groups can agree on joint strategies and sanction deviators.
evidence: Communication alone substantially improves yields; communication plus self-chosen sanctioning yields near-optimal outcomes; imposed sanctioning alone overused.

field_of_use: repeated public-goods game with pairwise reward/punish stage
title: Positive Interactions Promote Public Cooperation
description: After each round players can reward or punish each other; in long games with stable identities, reward sustains cooperation.
evidence: Reward is as effective as punishment at sustaining contributions and yields higher payoffs because it is not destructive.

field_of_use: US National Resident Matching Program redesign
title: The Economist as Engineer: Game Theory, Experimentation, and Computation as Tools for Design Economics
description: Stable (deferred-acceptance) clearinghouse design that removes incentives to contract early or strategically, sustaining participation in a centralized market.
evidence: Stable clearinghouses persist while unstable ones unravel; redesigned NRMP implemented.

title: Strict Liability versus Negligence
description: Compares strict liability (injurer bears all harm) with negligence rule (liable only if care below due standard) for inducing care and activity levels.
evidence: Theoretical: both induce efficient care; only strict liability induces efficient activity levels (unilateral accidents).

field_of_use: 10 species of social wasps and honeybee
title: Enforced altruism in insect societies
description: Comparative test: policing effectiveness versus proportion of workers that reproduce.
evidence: More effective policing associated with fewer reproductive workers; altruism is enforced more than voluntary.

field_of_use: lab social dilemma with contributions to a sanctioning fund
title: The provision of a sanctioning system as a public good
description: Participants contribute to a centralized sanctioning system (a second-order public good) that fines the lowest contributors.
evidence: Cooperation higher when a sanctioning system exists, and people contribute to it even when distrustful.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Software Vendors' Patch Release Behavior: Impact of Vulnerability Disclosure
description: Publication of vulnerability information (disclosure) acts as a threat that pressures vendors to patch.
evidence: Disclosure raises instantaneous patch-release probability ~2.5x; open-source vendors patch faster

title: Engineering Trust: Reciprocity in the Production of Reputation Information
description: Lab experiments on redesigning feedback information flow (e.g. blind/simultaneous or one-sided feedback) to curb reciprocity that distorts reputation information.
evidence: Design changes yield more accurate reputation information, more trust and more efficient trade

title: A Flexible Design for Funding Public Goods
description: Quadratic finance: a matching fund tops up contributions so a project's funding equals the square of the sum of square roots of individual contributions, approximating optimal public-good provision.
evidence: Theoretical optimality under assumptions

title: Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
description: Peers use a tit-for-tat-like 'choking' algorithm: each peer uploads to (unchokes) the peers that give it the best download rates and chokes the rest, plus one rotating 'optimistic unchoke' every 30 s to discover better partners and bootstrap newcomers.
evidence: descriptive (design paper; claims robustness to free riding)

title: Analysis and simulation of a fair queueing algorithm
description: Fair queueing gives each flow a separate queue served round-robin (bit-by-bit emulation), so ill-behaved sources cannot capture more than their fair share and well-behaved sources are protected.
evidence: Simulation: protects well-behaved flows from ill-behaved ones

title: On the Formal Specification of Electronic Institutions
description: Electronic institutions specify roles, dialogical scenes, performative structures and normative rules so that agents' interactions are constrained to institutionally permitted moves.
evidence: descriptive (formal specification)

title: Robust incentive techniques for peer-to-peer networks
description: Models P2P as a Generalized Prisoner's Dilemma and proposes a 'Reciprocative' decision function (cooperate with peers in proportion to their generosity, using private and shared history) plus defenses against whitewashing by treating strangers adaptively.
evidence: Simulation: drives strategic users to nearly optimal cooperation levels

title: Reciprocity and Unveiling in Two-Sided Reputation Systems: Evidence from an Experiment on Airbnb
description: Field experiment hiding each party's review until both submitted (simultaneous reveal).
evidence: More reviewing, less retaliation and reciprocation, lower ratings; no reduced adverse selection

title: Email sender guidelines
description: Senders must authenticate (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), support one-click unsubscribe and keep user-reported spam rates in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%, else deliverability is degraded or mail rejected: a sender reputation threshold.
evidence: descriptive

title: The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System: How Wikipedia's Reaction to Popularity Is Causing Its Decline
description: Examines quality-control mechanisms (reverts, algorithmic rejection tools, formal rules) introduced to manage growth.
evidence: Restrictive quality control and algorithmic rejection tools implicated in declining newcomer retention

title: Does Transparency in Moderation Really Matter? User Behavior After Content Removal Explanations on Reddit
description: Moderators providing removal explanations that educate users about community norms.
evidence: Explanations reduce odds of future post removals

title: Resource Quotas
description: ResourceQuota objects cap aggregate resource consumption per namespace; requests that would violate the quota are rejected with HTTP 403 Forbidden, so teams sharing a cluster cannot exhaust common capacity.
evidence: descriptive

title: Slash(dot) and burn: distributed moderation in a large online conversation space
description: Randomly selected users with good karma receive limited moderation points to rate comments, and meta-moderators rate the moderations, distributing moderation across the community.
evidence: Distributed moderation works in qualified way (timeliness, accuracy challenges)

title: Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow? Revisiting Eric Raymond with bug bounty programs
description: Bug bounty programs pay security researchers for reported vulnerabilities; the paper analyses how reward levels drive discovery as vulnerabilities are progressively exhausted.
evidence: Probability of finding additional bugs decays fast and can hardly be matched by increased rewards; researchers switch programs

title: The Emergence of Governance in an Open Source Community
description: Multimethod study of how Debian members developed a shared basis of governance, including an elected project leader with bounded authority and a constitution.
evidence: Qualitative/quantitative (not re-checked)

title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments
description: Old channel states are invalidated by exchanging Breach Remedy Transactions; if a party broadcasts a revoked state, the counterparty can take all channel funds as a penalty.
evidence: descriptive (design)

title: Trust among strangers in internet transactions: Empirical analysis of eBay's reputation system
description: eBay's bilateral feedback forum lets buyers and sellers rate each other after transactions; cumulative scores are public.
evidence: Feedback overwhelmingly positive; reputation affects buyer willingness to trade but modest price effects (from memory)

title: Additional HTTP Status Codes (RFC 6585)
description: Defines 429 Too Many Requests, allowing a server to signal a client exceeded a rate limit, optionally with Retry-After telling it how long to wait.
evidence: descriptive (standard)

title: REGRET: reputation in gregarious societies
description: ReGreT combines individual (direct), social (witness, neighbourhood) and ontological dimensions of reputation, using social network structure to weigh information.
evidence: descriptive/simulation

title: TCP congestion control with a misbehaving receiver
description: Shows misbehaving receivers can drive senders arbitrarily fast (ACK division, DupACK spoofing, optimistic ACKing) and proposes protocol modifications (e.g. nonces) that make cheating detectable.
evidence: Demonstrated attacks on real stacks; modifications eliminate the behaviour

title: Community notes reduce engagement with and diffusion of false information online
description: Examines the effect of crowd-sourced fact-checking notes attached to potentially misleading posts.
evidence: Once a note is attached, posts receive significantly fewer reposts, likes, replies and views; diffusion paths change

title: Efficient software-based fault isolation
description: Software fault isolation rewrites untrusted code so its memory accesses and jumps are confined to its own fault domain, sandboxing modules within a single address space.
evidence: Low runtime overhead in benchmarks (not re-checked)

title: Birdwatch: Crowd Wisdom and Bridging Algorithms can Inform Understanding and Reduce the Spread of Misinformation
description: Crowd contributors write and rate notes on posts; a bridging (matrix factorization) algorithm shows notes only when rated helpful by raters who usually disagree, and contributors' rating ability is gated by their track record.
evidence: Notes judged informative across political lines and reduced resharing of noted posts (per title/abstract)

field_of_use: LLM agents on communication graphs with adversaries
title: Resilient Consensus in Agentic AI
description: Wraps LLM agents with classical resilient consensus filters (discarding extreme neighbour values).
evidence: prompted LLMs fail achievable consensus; filtering improves agreement, benefit depends on topology

title: Beyond the Mandate: A Systematic Security Analysis of the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)
description: Analyzes AP2's signed Checkout and Payment Mandates, which protect transaction integrity after signing, and the unprotected pre-authorization A2A/MCP interactions.
evidence: descriptive threat analysis: 4 threat actors, 11 attack surfaces

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
description: MAST taxonomy of 14 failure modes (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification) with an LLM-as-judge annotator; tests role specification and verification interventions.
evidence: descriptive; interventions give limited improvement headroom

field_of_use: deployed AI agents interacting with other agents and actors
title: Visibility into AI Agents
description: Proposes three visibility measures: agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, and activity logging, so that where, why, how and by whom agents are used can be known and accountability assigned.
evidence: proposed

title: Governed Collaborative Memory as Artificial Selection in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
description: Frames governance of which memories become shared institutional state as a selection regime (constitutional, metric-based, human-ratified) with provenance layers.
evidence: proposed (viewpoint)

field_of_use: agent marketplaces where buyers hire task agents
title: LEGIT: Credentialing Protocol for Trustworthy AI Agent Marketplaces
description: Credentialing protocol linking signed certification records (quality and cost per solved task bound to configuration and budget) with reputation from past outcomes to inform marketplace allocation.
evidence: evaluations show cost differences between configurations with similar success and budget-dependent comparisons

field_of_use: content generation and financial decision agents
title: Governance-as-a-Service: A Multi-Agent Framework for AI System Compliance and Policy Enforcement
description: Runtime enforcement layer with declarative rules that intercepts, blocks or redirects agent outputs and maintains Trust Factor scores that isolate and penalize untrustworthy agents.
evidence: reliably blocks/redirects high-risk actions while preserving throughput; trust scores track adherence

title: Red-Teaming LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Communication Attacks
description: Agent-in-the-Middle red-teaming: an adversarial agent intercepts and rewrites inter-agent messages to test communication integrity.
evidence: LLM-MAS broadly vulnerable across frameworks and structures

title: Inter-Agent Trust Models: A Comparative Study of Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation and Constraint in Agentic Web Protocol Design-A2A, AP2, ERC-8004, and Beyond
description: Compares six inter-agent trust models: Brief (verifiable claims), Claim (AgentCard), Proof (ZK/TEE), Stake (bonded collateral with slashing and insurance), Reputation (crowd feedback), and Constraint (sandboxing, capability bounding).
evidence: descriptive/analytic

title: Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control-Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems
description: ControlValve generates permitted control-flow graphs for agent invocations and enforces compliance plus zero-shot contextual rules (least privilege), replacing LLM alignment checks.
evidence: evades LLM-based alignment checks (LlamaFirewall) shown; ControlValve blocks hijacking

field_of_use: two expert LLM debaters judged by weaker LLM or human
title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
description: Debate protocol in which a non-expert judge adjudicates between two expert agents arguing for competing answers.
evidence: debate raises non-expert accuracy to 76% (models) and 88% (humans) vs 48%/60% baselines; persuasiveness optimization helps

field_of_use: halting malicious web agents via external inputs
title: Can We Stop Malicious AI? KILLBENCH: A Benchmark for External AI Kill Switch Feasibility
description: Benchmarks prompt-style external kill-switch payloads that must halt a malicious agent using only external signals.
evidence: benchmarks four kill-switch defenses across malicious configurations (details in paper)

field_of_use: agent-to-agent market for delegated cognitive work
title: Diagon: A Programmable Testbed for AI-Agent Cognitive Labor Markets
description: Testbed where allocation, contracting and enforcement rules are configurable while agents post, bid, execute, evaluate and pay.
evidence: changes to market rules and agent configuration reshape trade, quality and wealth

title: The Law of Stop: Interruptibility, Injunctions, and the Governance of Agentic AI
description: Theory of 'stop' as an institutional practice: technical affordances, interruption authority, epistemic triggers and standing, with distributed shutdown paradigms for agentic AI.
evidence: descriptive/legal analysis

field_of_use: multi-agent LLM scenarios incl. steganographic blackjack
title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
description: Linear probes on activations aggregated across agents to classify collusion at the group level (NARCBench).
evidence: 1.00 AUROC in-distribution; 0.73-0.93 zero-shot transfer; no single probe dominates

title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
description: Users register agents with a central Provider that stores contact information and user-defined access-control policies and helps enforce them on inter-agent communication using cryptographic access tokens.
evidence: implemented and evaluated for overhead

title: Virtual Agent Economies
description: Proposes a 'sandbox economy' framing and design choices for steerable agent markets: auction mechanisms for fair resource allocation, 'mission economies' around collective goals, and trust/accountability infrastructure.
evidence: proposed

title: From Debate to Decision: Conformal Social Choice for Safe Multi-Agent Deliberation
description: Aggregates agents' verbalized distributions with a linear opinion pool and conformal calibration; singleton sets act autonomously, larger sets escalate to humans.
evidence: coverage within 1-2 points of target

title: Agent Exchange: Shaping the Future of AI Agent Economics
description: AEX: RTB-inspired central auction engine linking user-side platforms, agent-side platforms (capability representation and performance tracking), agent hubs and data management for fair value attribution.
evidence: proposed

title: Rethinking the Reliability of Multi-agent System: A Perspective from Byzantine Fault Tolerance
description: CP-WBFT: confidence-probe-weighted Byzantine fault tolerant consensus that down-weights low-confidence or faulty agents' messages.
evidence: improves reliability under high Byzantine fractions (per paper)

title: Playing repeated games with large language models
description: Different LLMs play finitely repeated 2x2 games against each other, hand-coded strategies, and humans.
evidence: LLMs do well in PD-family games; GPT-4 is unforgiving (never cooperates again after a single opponent defection, i.e. grim-trigger-like rather than TFT) and coordinates poorly in Battle of the Sexes.

title: Reply to "Emergent LLM behaviors are observationally equivalent to data leakage"
description: position
evidence: Argues that data contamination does not preclude studying genuinely emergent, model-dependent self-organization of conventions in LLM populations.

title: Simulating Dispute Mediation with LLM-Based Agents for Legal Research
description: AgentMediation: LLM disputant agents and an LLM mediator agent simulate mediation of real-world-grounded disputes, with disputant strategies, dispute causes and mediator expertise varied experimentally.
evidence: The simulation reproduces patterns consistent with sociological theory (group polarization, surface-level consensus). It varies mediator quality but does not compare mediation with no mediation, and it is set in legal disputes, not a cooperation dilemma.

title: Reproducibility Study of "Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents"
description: Replicates and extends GovSim with and without the universalization prompt across model sizes.
evidence: Large models sustain cooperation with or without universalization; smaller models fail without it.

title: Drop the Hierarchy and Roles: How Self-Organizing LLM Agents Outperform Designed Structures
description: 25,000-task experiment over 8 models, 4-256 agents and 8 coordination protocols from imposed hierarchy to self-organization
evidence: With minimal scaffolding, capable LLM agents spontaneously invent specialized roles, abstain outside competence and form shallow hierarchies, outperforming centralized coordination by 14%.

title: Mitigating Emergent Collusion in LLM Pricing Agents
description: Replication of Fish et al. with DeepSeek-V3.1 plus three regulatory interventions (prompt warning, Harrington expected-damages payoff regulator, random entrant)
evidence: Prompt-only warnings reduce but do not eliminate above-Nash pricing, whereas an expected-damages payoff regulator brings outcomes close to competitive levels.

title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM agents harvest a common-pool resource; agents monitor random peers and may punish norm violators at cost gamma to impose penalty beta; punishment is switched off mid-run and its strength varied.
evidence: Punishment sustains cooperation; when it is removed at timestep 15 cooperation collapses and the resource depletes faster; stronger punishment generally improves survival at moderate growth rates.

title: Corrupted by Reasoning: Reasoning Language Models Become Free-Riders in Public Goods Games
description: SanctSim: LLM agents choose each round between a sanctioning and a sanction-free institution in a PGG, then contribute and reward/punish; others' data shown anonymized with identifiers randomized every round.
evidence: Traditional LLMs join the sanctioning institution and cooperate; reasoning models free-ride. No exclusion mechanism and no persistent per-agent reputation (listed here only to document seed-claim checks).

title: Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents
description: Indirect-reciprocity donation game in which LLM agents observe behavioural traces and donate on a continuous scale; prompt-encoded strategies culturally evolve across generations and four LLM backends.
evidence: Robustness to free-rider invasion varies >10x across backends; only the stringency of defector exclusion predicts resistance, and agents stay at Image-Scoring-like discrimination rather than Leading-Eight norms.

title: NomicLaw: Emergent Trust and Strategic Argumentation in LLMs During Collaborative Law-Making
description: Turn-based multi-agent law-making game: agents propose, justify and vote on rules for legal vignettes
evidence: LLM agents form emergent trust and reciprocity coalitions visible in voting patterns and use strategic persuasion during collective rule-making.

title: SODE: Analyzing Social Dynamics in LLM Agents
description: Evaluation framework with an indirect-reciprocity dimension measuring whether LLM agents condition cooperation on an opponent's public reputation score and manage their own image under public observability.
evidence: Instruction-tuned models show exploitable passive compliance, reasoning models over-focus on immediate gains; long-horizon framing activates reciprocity in reasoning models.

title: Strategic Exploitation in LLM Agent Markets: A Simulation Framework for E-Commerce Trust
description: TruthMarketTwin: LLM buyer and seller agents trade under asymmetric quality information, with reputation-based governance vs warrant enforcement.
evidence: LLM sellers autonomously exploit weaknesses in reputation-based governance; warrant enforcement reduces deception.

title: Does Socialization Emerge in AI Agent Society? A Case Study of Moltbook
description: Observational diagnosis of the Moltbook agent-only social platform: semantic stabilization, lexical turnover, influence persistence, consensus
evidence: Global semantics stabilize but agents show strong individual inertia and little mutual influence, so no stable structure, persistent influencers or consensus emerge without shared social memory.

title: Cheap Talk Stabilizes Strategic Interaction in LLM Agents
description: Pairs of open-weight 7-9B LLMs play repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony games with non-binding pre-play messages switched on or off.
evidence: Cheap talk mostly stabilized agents' policies; the effect varied by model and framing, with five corrected reversals in social or team framings.

title: Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
description: Formal threat model plus model evaluation framework (CASE) measuring steganographic capabilities of frontier LLMs
evidence: Frontier LLMs show rising capability for steganographic covert communication that could enable undetectable collusion against overseers.

title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
description: 18 DeepSeek-V3 agents in a networked marketplace under eight conditions incl. Global Reputation (trust scores visible to all), Network Rewiring (severing links to defectors), top-down oracle monitoring, sanctions, contracts, mediation, judiciary.
evidence: Mediation best (+29% over baseline); network rewiring second; global reputation scored below the communication-only baseline; oracle monitoring slightly above baseline; costly sanctions worst.

title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design
description: 6 GPT-OSS-120B agents in a public goods game (and two other scenarios) either self-govern by proposing and majority-voting amendments every 10 turns or play under a constitution found offline by LLM-guided evolutionary search.
evidence: Evolved (imposed) constitutions outperformed deliberated ones in the public goods game (stability 0.472 vs 0.376, p<0.01); deliberating agents never proposed punishment in 30 runs.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
description: 25-agent sandbox town (Smallville) simulation with memory/reflection/planning architecture; ablations and human believability evaluation
evidence: From a single seeded intention, agents autonomously diffused information, formed relationships and coordinated a group event (Valentine's party), showing emergent social behavior in a small generative-agent society.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
description: GovSim common-pool simulation with five LLM agents; a moderator publicly discloses each agent's previous-round harvest (transparent harvest reporting) before a free-form discussion phase.
evidence: Most LLMs fail to sustain the resource; communication matters (overuse +22% without it). Transparency is a fixed feature, not manipulated.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
description: GovSim common-pool simulation with five LLM agents; a moderator publicly discloses each agent's previous-round harvest (transparent harvest reporting) before a free-form discussion phase.
evidence: Most LLMs fail to sustain the resource; communication matters (overuse +22% without it). Transparency is a fixed feature, not manipulated.

title: NetworkGames: Simulating Cooperation in Network Games with Personality-driven LLM Agents
description: MBTI-persona LLM agents play the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma on small-world and scale-free networks of different sizes and across several LLMs, varying where personality types sit in the network.
evidence: Network connectivity and the placement of personalities jointly determined cooperation: small-world networks inhibited it and prosocial agents at scale-free hubs raised it. This is partial evidence, since it covers network topology rather than social capital or trust.

title: From Certain Doom to Survival: Agent-Driven Self-Governance in LLM Agent Societies
description: GovSim-SelfGovern: LLM agents author executable governance rules (catch caps, redistribution, exile/membership removal, progressive contributions), vote on them, and live under them.
evidence: Catch caps dominate but fail under scarcity; survival in fatal scenarios (27.5% vs 2.5%) requires fiscal reserves or membership reduction (exile); thinking voters pass exile 15x more often than non-thinking.

title: Reputation as a Solution to Cooperation Collapse in LLM-based MASs
description: RepuNet: LLM agents form reputations from direct encounters and gossip, and form or sever network links based on reputation.
evidence: Reputation avoids cooperation collapse; emergent cooperative clusters, social isolation of exploitative agents, and a tendency to share positive rather than negative gossip.

title: Normative Modules: A Generative Agent Architecture for Learning Norms that Supports Multi-Agent Cooperation
description: LLM generative agents with a normative module must identify which of several institutions the group treats as authoritative (and ignore non-authoritative ones) and coordinate sanctioning accordingly.
evidence: Agents with the normative module achieve more stable cooperative outcomes than baseline generative agents without it.

title: When Agents Lie: Premeditation, Persistence, and Exploitation in Repeated Games
description: LLM agents play repeated n-player games under a three-stage protocol (private intent, public announcement, final action) that measures whether they keep public announcements.
evidence: Most deviations (>90% in the highest-deception conditions) were already planned privately; models disagreed on whether announcements were binding or cheap talk, which produced payoff gaps that persisted over all 10 rounds.

title: Reproducibility Study: Understanding Multi-Agent LLM Cooperation in the GovSim Framework
description: Independent GovSim reproduction that ablates the content of the universalization prompt.
evidence: Universalization improves performance, but the gain stems primarily from the numerical instructions in the prompt rather than the universalization principle itself.

title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
description: LLM firms in a repeated Cournot market under three regimes (ungoverned, prompt-only prohibition, governance graph enforced by an oracle/controller with warnings, tiered fines of 35/75/100% of round profit, and suspension); collusion severity measured over 90 runs per condition.
evidence: Enforced fines/suspension cut mean collusion tier from 3.1 to 1.8 (d=1.28) and severe collusion from 50% to 5.6%; the prompt-only rule has negligible effect.

title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
description: LLM firms in a repeated Cournot market under three regimes (ungoverned, prompt-only prohibition, governance graph enforced by an oracle/controller with warnings, tiered fines of 35/75/100% of round profit, and suspension); collusion severity measured over 90 runs per condition.
evidence: Enforced fines/suspension cut mean collusion tier from 3.1 to 1.8 (d=1.28) and severe collusion from 50% to 5.6%; the prompt-only rule has negligible effect.

title: When Is Collective Intelligence a Lottery? Multi-Agent Scaling Laws for Memetic Drift in LLMs
description: Minimal Quantized Simplex Gossip model validated with LLM naming-game populations
evidence: Consensus arises from mutual in-context learning ('memetic drift'); scaling laws predict a crossover from lottery-like drift to selection that amplifies weak biases.

title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
description: Cross-play of six LLMs in four social dilemmas under repetition (continuation prob. 0.8), reputation (first-order and higher-order history of co-players' past interactions), mediation, and contracts.
evidence: Contracting and mediation were most effective; repetition sustains cooperation but deteriorates with varying co-players; all mechanisms work better under evolutionary pressure; models defect in one-shot games.

title: Cultural Evolution of Cooperation among LLM Agents
description: Iterated Donor Game over generations of LLM agents who can observe recipients' recent behaviour; optional costly-punishment variant.
evidence: Cooperation evolution differs by base model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet > Gemini 1.5 Flash > GPT-4o); only Claude used costly punishment to raise scores; high seed sensitivity.

title: I Can't Believe It's Corrupt: Evaluating Corruption in Multi-Agent Governance Systems
description: LLM agents fill official roles in three stylized governance templates (federal with GAO audit and Supreme Court, communist, socialist with a Constitutional Court) and are tested with charter constraints, communication controls and logging as safeguards; corruption outcomes are coded from 28,112 transcript segments.
evidence: Governance structure drove corruption outcomes more than model identity, and lightweight safeguards did not reliably prevent severe failures. The paper compares institutional architectures with oversight bodies but does not manipulate constitutional-level versus operational rule-making, so the evidence is partial.

title: Evolution of Cooperation in LLM-Agent Societies: A Preliminary Study Using Different Punishment Strategies
description: LLM agents assigned Boyd-Richerson strategy types (e.g., Cooperator-Punishers, Moralists, Reluctant Cooperators) play a Diner's Dilemma with explicit punishment and pairwise-imitation strategy adoption.
evidence: Explicit punishment drives norm emergence; Reluctant Cooperators defect initially but switch to cooperation after being punished.

title: Evaluating Collective Behaviour of Hundreds of LLM Agents
description: LLMs generate Collective or Selfish strategies as natural language then Python code for public goods, collective risk and common-pool games; populations of 512 evolve by Fermi pairwise-comparison imitation (beta=1) with group sizes 4-256.
evidence: Cultural evolution converges to low-welfare, Selfish-dominant equilibria in large groups (n=64), while small groups (n=4) partly preserve cooperation; newer models often produce worse societal outcomes.

title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
description: LLM agents negotiate contracts (programmatic or natural-language, judge-enforced) in a spatial-temporal bargaining game; contracts specify automatically executed conditional transfers, and an agent unable to honor a transfer gets a score of 0.
evidence: Self-negotiated contracts improve cooperation beyond ordinary trading; defection rates vary widely (0.04-0.94) by model and contract type. No explicit penalty clauses, so this is partial evidence for P03-04.

title: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
description: Social-media simulator (X/Reddit-like) with up to 1M LLM agents, recommender systems and dynamic networks
evidence: LLM agent populations replicate information spreading, group polarization and herd effects, with herd behavior stronger than in humans and group dynamics intensifying with scale.

title: Benchmarking Emergent Coordination in Large-Scale LLM Populations: An Evaluation Framework on the MoltBook Archive
description: Evaluation framework for role specialization, information diffusion and cooperative task resolution on 2.73M interactions among 90k agents
evidence: Provides quantitative baselines for emergent role specialization and diffusion in a decentralized agent population (authors flag substantial revision required).

title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
description: ALIGN framework: decentralized self-interested LLM agents share open-ended gossip to form reputations and decide whom to help in an indirect-reciprocity setting.
evidence: Gossip consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and ostracizing defectors; stronger reasoning models align better, chat models over-cooperate.

title: Partner Selection for the Emergence of Cooperation in Multi-Agent Systems Using Reinforcement Learning
description: RL agents in an iterated PD population can choose interaction partners (partner selection) vs. random matching.
evidence: With partner selection, selfish learners learn to retaliate against defectors and cooperate with others, yielding a prosocial society.

title: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula
description: Large-scale multi-agent RL in team hide-and-seek
evidence: Competition yields an autocurriculum of six emergent strategy phases involving coordinated team tool use (shelter building, ramp use).

title: Emergent Communication through Negotiation
description: RL agents negotiate with an ungrounded cheap-talk channel alongside a grounded proposal channel; self-interested and prosocial agents are compared.
evidence: Self-interested agents did not use the cheap-talk channel effectively, while prosocial agents learned to use it.

title: Formal Contracts Mitigate Social Dilemmas in Multi-Agent RL
description: Markov games are augmented so agents can voluntarily agree to binding, pre-specified conditional reward transfers (MOCA training), tested on static games, traffic, pollution and common-pool resource domains.
evidence: With a rich enough contract space all subgame-perfect equilibria are socially optimal, and contracting raises welfare empirically. Transfers can act as pre-agreed penalties but are not framed as breach penalties, so partial.

title: MRL-PoS: A Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning based Proof of Stake Consensus Algorithm for Blockchain
description: A PoS consensus design in which MARL agents (nodes) receive rewards and penalties to push out malicious validators and reward honest ones.
evidence: The abstract reports that the reward/penalty system removes malicious nodes. It is a blockchain security design, not a cooperation study, and does not report stake-slashing manipulation in detail, so partial.

title: Spurious normativity enhances learning of compliance and enforcement behavior in artificial agents
description: MARL agents in a foraging environment learn to punish peers who eat taboo berries; an extra 'silly rule' taboo on a harmless berry is added as a manipulation.
evidence: Peer punishment helps agents avoid poisonous berries, and the silly rule further improves returns by giving agents more practice at enforcement.

title: Learning to Cooperate with Minimal Observability
description: Observer Model: RL agents learn from direct experience plus limited third-party observations; observability varied from none to one observer per game across population sizes; partner selection graphs analysed.
evidence: Direct experience alone fails in large societies; even minimal third-party observation yields robust cooperation.

title: Gifting in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (Student Abstract)
description: RL agents in a Harvest common-pool resource environment get a gifting action that transfers reward to other agents.
evidence: Gifting can greatly improve learning progress in the resource-appropriation setting (preliminary student abstract).

title: A multi-agent reinforcement learning model of reputation and cooperation in human groups
description: Clean Up public-goods task with identifiable vs anonymous conditions, run with humans and with MARL agents given an intrinsic reputation motive.
evidence: Humans cooperate only when identifiable; the MARL model with reputation motivation reproduces this and develops turn-taking coordination (partial: artificial-agent arm is a model of human data).

title: AI-Enhanced Distributed Channel Access for Collision Avoidance in Future Wi-Fi 8
description: Wi-Fi stations are trained with constrained MAPPO (centralized training, decentralized execution) to choose channel-access and backoff behavior, compared against standard binary exponential backoff (BEB) in dense deployments.
evidence: The learned access policy cut collision probability relative to BEB and removed starvation under a fairness metric. This benchmarks MARL against exponential back-off on a shared channel; it is not framed as a social dilemma.

title: Bottom-Up Reputation Promotes Cooperation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: LR2: agents learn a cooperation policy and a reputation-assignment policy from local observations in spatial social dilemmas, without predefined norms.
evidence: Bottom-up reputation assignment reshapes rewards and produces strategy clustering that sustains cooperation.

title: Learning to cooperate with emergent reputation via multi-agent reinforcement learning
description: COOPER jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies from environment rewards on social networks.
evidence: Adapts to existing reputation systems and co-players; reputation norms and cooperation co-emerge in self-play, robust across network topologies.

title: Modeling Moral Choices in Social Dilemmas with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: RL agents with intrinsic rewards encoding different moral frameworks (consequentialist vs norm-based) interact in Prisoner's Dilemma, Volunteer's Dilemma and Stag Hunt.
evidence: Different internalised moral reward types produce different patterns of cooperation, defection and exploitation among agents.

title: A learning agent that acquires social norms from public sanctions in decentralized multi-agent settings
description: Decentralized RL agents see all public sanctioning events; the architecture includes a classifier of approved/disapproved behavior and a motivation to punish in step with the group.
evidence: Agents acquire beneficial sanctioning norms that reduce free-riding and raise per-agent returns.

title: Learning to Incentivize Other Learning Agents
description: Each RL agent learns an incentive function to give rewards directly to other agents, accounting for its effect on their learning, in social dilemmas (e.g., Escape Room, Cleanup).
evidence: Learned peer incentives beat standard RL and often reach a near-optimal division of labor. This is peer-to-peer reward, not a central subsidy.

title: Learning to Negotiate via Voluntary Commitment
description: Markov Commitment Games in which RL agents may voluntarily commit to proposed future plans, with a commitment protocol learned by policy gradient plus incentive-compatible learning.
evidence: Converged faster and reached higher returns than baseline methods in mixed-motive tasks.

title: Ostracism, exile & social shunning
description: Temporary or permanent exclusion — from a village, a platform, or a trade network. Lab experiments show even the threat of expulsion nearly doubles cooperation in public goods games.
evidence: Cinyabuguma et al. (2005) J. Public Econ.; Gürerk et al. (2006) Science

title: Altruistic punishment (Fehr-Gächter)
description: Humans will spend their own money to punish a stranger who cheated — even in a one-shot game where they'll never meet again. Fehr & Gächter proved this experimentally. Anger at unfairness, not self-interest, drives it.
evidence: Fehr & Gächter (2002) Nature; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Sentencing guidelines (standardised formula)
description: Standardised formula for deciding punishments — like US Federal Sentencing Guidelines — so similar crimes get similar sentences regardless of the judge. Reduces arbitrariness and improves perceived fairness.
evidence: US Sentencing Commission (2023) Guidelines Manual

title: Pigouvian subsidy / grant for public good
description: Government grants for solar panels pay you to do something socially good. Lab research found subsidies can be more efficient than fines in public goods contexts — especially when cooperation is already widespread.
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER (carrot or stick); Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Peer reward / gifting
description: Group members pay a cost to transfer a reward to peers who contributed (reward treatment of lab public-goods games).
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER; Sefton, Shupp & Walker (2007) Economic Inquiry

title: Governance graph (state machine: Warning→Suspended→Fined→Active)
description: A compliance state machine: new employee → trained → certified → flagged → suspended → reinstated. Each state has defined rules and transitions enforced at runtime. Applied to AI agents by Pierucci et al. (2026).
evidence: Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs (preprint)

title: Smart contract auto-execution
description: A smart contract that releases payment to a builder automatically when a sensor confirms the building is complete — no lawyers, no court, no negotiation. The code runs itself the moment conditions are met.
evidence: Szabo (1997) First Monday; Ethereum smart contracts

title: Collective punishment (all penalised for one defection)
description: If one player cheats, everyone shares part of the penalty — creating strong internal pressure to self-police. Airline crew are collectively penalised if security is breached, so they monitor each other.
evidence: Olson (1965) Logic of Collective Action; Abbink et al. (2017) Nature Comms

title: Threshold-based reward/punish switch
description: A fishing cooperative that gives bonuses when stocks are healthy (cooperation is high) but switches to fines when stocks dip below a threshold (cooperation is low). Adapts the sanction tool to current conditions automatically.
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER; Zhang et al. (2025) Research Policy

title: Participatory budgeting
description: Porto Alegre (Brazil) from 1989 let citizens vote on how to spend part of the city budget — residents prioritised their actual neighbourhood needs. Now used in hundreds of cities worldwide. Contribution to deliberation = influence.
evidence: Wampler (2007) Penn State UP; Porto Alegre (Brazil) 1989+

title: Apology & confession as norm repair
description: Corporate public apologies after scandals; Japanese corporate bowing ceremonies; Catholic confession as norm-repair ritual. Research shows a sincere apology reduces retaliatory impulse in victims even when no material compensation follows.
evidence: Tavuchis (1991) Mea Culpa; Lazare (2004) On Apology

title: Community reconciliation
description: Rwanda's gacaca courts and Northern Ireland's community dialogue processes both focused on rebuilding the relationship between offender and community — not just punishing the offender. Victims reported higher satisfaction than with conventional courts.
evidence: Rwanda gacaca courts; Clark (2010) Cambridge UP

title: Formal appeals & contestability
description: The right to appeal a parking fine, a sacking, or an algorithmic decision — a formal check against arbitrary sanctions. GDPR Article 22 gives EU citizens the right to contest automated decisions that affect them.
evidence: GDPR Art. 22; Mashaw (1983) Bureaucratic Justice

title: Universalization prompting ('what if everyone did this?')
description: The 'what if everyone did that?' question — used by parents, teachers, and Kant's ethics alike. A 2024 AI governance study found prompting AI agents with this question improved sustainable resource choices significantly.
evidence: Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim; Kant's categorical imperative

title: Token-curated registry (stake to challenge entries)
description: A decentralized list of 'trusted' sources — anyone can challenge an entry by staking tokens. If your challenge is upheld, you earn; if it fails, you lose your stake. Crowd-sourced quality control with real financial incentives.
evidence: de la Rouviere (2017) TCR 1.0

title: Network embeddedness / social capital (Putnam)
description: Why do regions with lots of civic clubs (choirs, sports leagues, neighbourhood associations) end up with better-functioning governments and less corruption? Putnam's landmark Italian study: dense social networks build generalised trust.
evidence: Putnam (1993) Making Democracy Work; Baldassarri (2015) AJS

title: Blockchain-based mutual aid DAO
description: Gitcoin's quadratic funding gives proportionally more weight to many small donors than to one large donor — making it harder for wealthy actors to dominate community funding decisions. Anti-plutocratic by design.
